subject: physical-education
essentialQuestion: What makes an activity one that people actually want to come back to?

prompts.prompt: Explain the critical features or key principle of safety responsibility toward yourself and others in your own words.
Demonstrate or fully describe rules, officiating basics, and honest self-calling using a version your body and setting allow. A described or adapted version earns full credit.
Apply winning and losing without changing how you treat people in a new situation and explain the decision or adjustment you made.
Analyze a plausible technique fault, tactical error, or unsafe choice involving designing for inclusion rather than adding it afterward; correct it and explain why.
Connect giving and receiving feedback about performance, never about bodies with conflict during activity and how to resolve it and explain how one affects the other.

Present the strongest evidence from the unit task: Redesign a standard activity so that three people with different mobility, experience, and confidence profiles can all participate meaningfully in the same game, and defend each design choice.
Identify one thing you can now do or direct yourself, one adjustment that improved it, and one next goal you set for yourself.

adaptationChoices: The redesign may be written, diagrammed, described aloud, or trialed practically. Practical trial is optional.
accommodationNote: Access supports may change format, pacing, intensity, range, equipment, setting, or response mode without changing the standard being assessed. An adapted or described performance is full credit, not partial credit.
neverRequires: This task never requires body weight, height, BMI, or body-fat percentage.
This task never requires calorie counting or a diet or weight-loss goal.
This task never requires disclosing private medical history, a diagnosis, or sexual history.
This task never requires a photograph, video, or voice recording of the learner as proof.
This task never requires a public performance or an audience.
